title: There are questions people whisper in the dark… the kind they don’t bring to church, the kind they don’t type publicly, the kind they carry like a secret weight pressing against their chest.
paragraphs: There are questions people whisper in the dark… the kind they don’t bring to church, the kind they don’t type publicly, the kind they carry like a secret weight pressing against their chest.
“Does God care about my sexual preferences?”
Not the polished version. Not the theological version. The real one.

Does He look at me differently?
Does He feel disappointed?
Does He still want me… or just a version of me that doesn’t exist yet?
You don’t ask that question unless something inside you is already trembling.
And maybe that’s where this needs to start—not with answers, but with honesty.
Because the Bible never pretends humans are clean before they come to God. It shows the opposite.

David wasn’t clean.
The woman at the well wasn’t clean.
The woman caught in adultery wasn’t clean.
And yet… Jesus didn’t walk away.
He walked closer.

In John 8:7, when everyone was ready to stone her, Jesus said in Greek,
“Ὁ ἀναμάρτητος ὑμῶν πρῶτος ἐπ’ αὐτὴν βαλέτω λίθον”
“He who is without sin among you, let him throw the first stone.”
And one by one… they dropped their stones.
But don’t miss what happens next.
“Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.” (John 8:11)
There it is.
Grace… and truth.
Not one without the other.
Because God absolutely cares about your sexual life… but not the way most people think.

He doesn’t care so He can shame you.
He cares because He made you.

In Genesis 1:27, the Hebrew says,
“וַיִּבְרָא אֱלֹהִים אֶת־הָאָדָם בְּצַלְמוֹ”
“Vayyivra Elohim et-ha’adam b’tzalmo”
“So God created man in His image.”

That means your body isn’t random.
Your desires aren’t meaningless.
Your identity isn’t self-invented.
You were designed.
And anything designed… has intention.
So when people ask, “Does God care about my sexual preferences?” what they’re really asking is:
“Does God care about what I do with the parts of me that feel the most personal… the most powerful… the most defining?”
Yes.
Deeply.
Because sexuality isn’t just behavior in Scripture—it’s covenant language. It’s tied to faithfulness, to union, to reflection of something divine.
Ephesians 5:31–32 reveals something shocking:
“This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church.”
Marriage… intimacy… union… it was never just physical.
It was always pointing to Jesus.
Which means when sexuality is pulled outside of God’s design, it doesn’t just break a rule… it distorts a reflection.
And yet—this is where most people get it wrong—
God’s response to distortion is not abandonment.
It’s redemption.
Look at the Samaritan woman in John 4.

Five husbands.
Living with a man who wasn’t her husband.
If anyone had a complicated sexual history… it was her.
And Jesus meets her alone at a well.

No audience.
No performance.
No condemnation.
He speaks directly into her reality:
“You have had five husbands, and the one you now have is not your husband.” (John 4:18)
He doesn’t ignore truth.
But He doesn’t leave her there either.
He offers her something deeper than validation… and something more powerful than rejection.
“Living water.”
And that moment… that one encounter… turns her from someone hiding at a well into someone running back to a city, saying:
“Come, see a man who told me everything I ever did.”
She wasn’t canceled.
She was called.
So let’s answer it clearly now.
Does God care about your sexual preferences?
Yes.
But not because He’s obsessed with controlling you.
Because He’s committed to restoring you.
Because sin—any sin, not just sexual—separates us from the life we were created for.

Romans 3:23 says in Greek:
“πάντες γὰρ ἥμαρτον”
“For all have sinned.”

Not some.
Not a category.
Not a group you can point at to feel better about yourself.
All.
Which means this isn’t about “your sin vs their sin.”
It’s about all of us standing in need of the same Savior.
Jesus didn’t come to rank sins.
He came to carry them.

1 Peter 2:24 says,
“He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree.”

Every hidden struggle.
Every identity confusion.
Every moment you felt divided inside yourself.
He carried it.
So the real question isn’t, “Does God care about your sexual preferences?”
The real question is:
Will you trust Him enough to let Him define what’s good for your soul?
Because the hardest part isn’t admitting struggle.
It’s surrendering authority.
And that’s where transformation begins.
Not when you pretend you’re fine.
But when you stop hiding.
Maybe you’ve been trying to reconcile two voices inside you.
One that says, “This is who I am.”
And another whispering, “But is this who God created me to be?”
That tension… that discomfort… that quiet unrest…
That’s not rejection.
That’s invitation.
An invitation to come closer, not run further.
To wrestle honestly, not silence conviction.
To let Jesus—not culture, not feelings, not fear—be the One who defines truth.
Because the Gospel doesn’t say, “Stay as you are.”
It says, “Come as you are… and be made new.”

2 Corinthians 5:17 in Greek:
“καινὴ κτίσις”
“a new creation.”

Not adjusted.
Not slightly improved.
New.
And that kind of transformation… it doesn’t happen through arguments.
It happens through encounter.
Through relationship.
Through surrender.
Sit with it.
Be honest.
Because this isn’t about being perfect.
It’s about being real before a God who already sees everything… and still chooses to love you.
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
And don’t keep this to yourself.
You might be the reason they finally feel seen.
You’re going to need this reminder again when the questions come back.
And if you feel God pulling you deeper… not just into inspiration, but into real discipleship, accountability, and transformation…
Because supporting this mission isn’t just about content.
It’s about helping more people encounter Jesus without filters.
It’s about making sure the Gospel reaches the ones who feel too far gone.
If this message stirred something in you… don’t ignore it.
God isn’t pushing you away.
He’s calling you closer.
And the part of you you’re most afraid to bring to Him…
is the exact place He wants to redeem.
You don’t need to fix yourself before you come.
You need to come… so He can fix what you never could.
The place you thought disqualified you… might be the very place grace begins.
